title: The Wednesday Tesh Mbaabu Wrote RejaReja's Closing Chapter
dek: In April 2024, after two years of layoffs and market exits, MarketForce closed its shop-supply app RejaReja and its co-founder named the mistakes.

story.event: Closing the RejaReja B2B retail platform after layoffs and withdrawal from most of its markets
story.summary: On 17 April 2024 Tesh Mbaabu announced on his blog that MarketForce, the Kenyan start-up he co-founded with Mesongo Sibuti in 2018, would close RejaReja, its app for neighbourhood shops to order stock on credit. After a $40 million Series A in 2022, $8 million of committed equity never arrived; the company laid off about 250 people, cut delivery routes and in late 2023 left Nigeria, Rwanda and Tanzania, keeping RejaReja running only in Uganda. Mbaabu blamed thin margins and price wars, acknowledged the founders' own mistakes, and moved to the social-commerce start-up Chpter.
paragraphs: On Wednesday 17 April 2024, Tesh Mbaabu posted on his blog that RejaReja would close. “Unfortunately, that is our closing chapter,” he wrote. He and Mesongo Sibuti had started MarketForce in Kenya in 2018 as sales software for consumer brands. When the pandemic took most of their recurring revenue, they turned it into RejaReja, an app through which neighbourhood shops could order stock for next-day delivery and buy on credit.

Growth was fast. By Mbaabu's count RejaReja reached 21 cities in five countries, more than 800 staff and over 270,000 merchants. In February 2022 MarketForce raised a $40 million Series A of equity and debt. Then, he told TechCrunch, some investors who had signed did not pay: $8 million of the $20 million in equity never arrived, cutting the runway by more than eighteen months just as funding for African start-ups dried up.

What followed was a long series of cuts. By May 2023 there had been two rounds of layoffs, about 250 people in all; daily delivery routes had fallen from over 700 to 400; and some payments to staff and suppliers were late, though he said they were being kept informed. By late October it had left Nigeria, Rwanda and Tanzania, and TechCrunch reported that RejaReja would carry on only in Uganda, where margins were better.

It was not enough. Retail goods have razor-thin margins, he wrote, and the price wars never stop: “That’s always a race to the bottom.” After trying every possible tweak, he and Sibuti had to “look each other in the eye” and call it. He did not hide the mistakes. They had built for aggressive expansion on money that did not all come, and could have communicated faster about what was failing. Those mistakes, he wrote, had “such high financial and emotional costs for people who had bought the dream.”

He called the ending devastating, and wrote that the only way to lose was not to get back up. He and Sibuti moved to Chpter, a social-commerce start-up whose founders they had backed early, building tools for merchants who sell on WhatsApp and Instagram.

quote.text: I have not yet seen one who could perceive his faults, and inwardly accuse himself.
quote.source_title: The Analects of Confucius (from the Chinese Classics), tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #3330
quote.connection: Confucius complained that he had never met anyone who could see his own faults and accuse himself inwardly. Mbaabu's closing post did it in the open, naming the mistakes and who paid for them, while still insisting that the right answer was to try again.

reflection: Of everything in Mbaabu's post, the line that stays is not the one about margins. It is the admission that the founders could have communicated faster and more clearly about what was not working, and that people who had bought the dream paid for it. He wrote it while the loss was still raw, under his own name.

Most of what goes wrong in your working life will be far smaller than this. The pattern holds, though. Bad news held back for a better moment rarely gets lighter, and the people relying on you usually cope better with the truth early than with a surprise late.
invitation: Think of one piece of work that is not going to plan and that someone else is counting on. Tell that person today, in two plain sentences, where it really stands.

cross_checks.claim: On 17 April 2024 Mbaabu announced on his blog that RejaReja would close
MarketForce began in 2018 as sales software and pivoted to the RejaReja marketplace when the pandemic hit
At its peak RejaReja employed more than 800 people and served about 270,000 merchants
$8 million of committed Series A equity never arrived
In October 2023 MarketForce left Nigeria, Rwanda and Tanzania, with RejaReja continuing only in Uganda
Thin margins and price wars made RejaReja unsustainable

research_notes: Merchants: TechCabal says MarketForce supported 'over 1 million merchants', which matches the company's stated goal rather than its reach; Mbaabu's own post and TechCrunch (2024) both give over 270,000, which the story uses. Funding: TechCrunch (2024) gives $42.5 million raised in total, including a $40 million debt-and-equity Series A; TechCabal gives $40 million at a $100 million valuation; Mbaabu's post says investors committed $40 million. In 2023 Mbaabu told TechCrunch that $8 million of the $20 million equity was never wired; he did not name the investors and the story does not. The story says the company 'raised' a $40 million round as announced and then states the shortfall. Markets: TechCrunch's October 2023 headline says three markets were exited, but its text lists RejaReja discontinued in Kenya, Nigeria, Rwanda and Tanzania with Uganda kept (Kenya stayed headquarters); TechCrunch (2024) says all markets 'save for Uganda'. TechTrends Kenya (31 October 2023) names only Nigeria, Rwanda and Tanzania as exits and quotes Mbaabu that MarketForce was 'now just operational in Kenya and Uganda', which fits Kenya remaining headquarters and Chpter's base. The story therefore says MarketForce left Nigeria, Rwanda and Tanzania and that, as TechCrunch reported, RejaReja itself would carry on only in Uganda. Cities: Mbaabu says 21 cities; TechCrunch (2023) quotes him on 20 towns; the story uses his post. Chpter: TechCrunch calls it a spinout; Mbaabu's post says it was founded in 2021 by two other founders whom he and Sibuti had invested in, and that they joined forces; the story follows his account. TechCabal also reports difficulty meeting obligations to the credit partner Pezesha, since resolved between the companies; the story leaves it out rather than characterise a private settlement. The layoffs, delayed payments and the founders' acknowledged mistakes are given in Mbaabu's own words or attributed to him. His later blog bio describes a newer company (Cloud9 Money), outside this episode.
